extracted.intended_audience: American art patrons, artists (especially those studying in Europe), and literate readers interested in art criticism and Roman/Italian affairs.
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance on judging paintings and sculpture, advice for American patrons commissioning or supporting artists (esp. in Italy), and recommendations for selecting public monuments (e.g., equestrian statues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of design
rubrics_metrics.description: “The design of the picture is never original” (criticizing works that are merely pleasing transpositions of local hues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A picture should have an original design and convey something from the heart; mere pleasant coloring or faithful transcription of nature without original compositional thought is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coloring derived from thoughtful study rather than imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “His system of coloring is derived from a thoughtful study, not a mere imitation of nature, and shows the fineness of his organization.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good coloring arises from studied principles and organizational skill, not from slavish copying; coloring can reveal an artist’s intellectual method and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic feeling / spirit of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists should possess a “poetic heart” and produce a “transfusion of the spirit” of landscape rather than only copying scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape work should capture the inner, poetic quality of nature—its spirit and divinity—so that paintings go beyond literal views to communicate feeling and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to natural detail and intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cropsey is praised as “a reverent and careful student of nature in detail” whose pictures “are full of little, gentle signs of intimacy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close study of natural detail that produces signs of intimacy and quiet truthfulness is a virtue; however, detail should not substitute for larger poetic feeling when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of grouping and composition for multi-figure works
rubrics_metrics.description: Hicks’s drawing for a large picture of many figures: “the design is original and noble, the grouping highly effective.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex compositions the originality of the design and the effectiveness of grouping figures are key—good grouping produces noble, readable, and emotionally convincing scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to artist’s temperament and strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps a melancholy or tender subject suits him best; something rich, bold, and mellow is more adapted to call out the genius of Cranch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects consonant with an artist’s sensibilities; an artist’s temperament and strengths should guide subject selection to allow their best qualities to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture national / native character rather than slavish foreign copying
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer hopes to see “not only copies upon canvas of our magnificent scenes, but a transfusion of the spirit which is their divinity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American landscape painters should convey the distinctive spirit of their own country rather than merely reproducing foreign models; national character can be a source of originality and excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate duration and purpose of study abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: “The American landscape painter ought not to stay here very long. Yet a few years' study is precious” because in Italy nature has worked with man to instruct composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term study in artistic centers (a few years) is valuable to learn composition, the union of architecture/ruins/vegetation and harmony of forms, but prolonged residence risks losing one’s native vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility and compositional balance at a distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Goethe: “a fine work of art will always have, at a distance, where its details cannot be discerned, a beautiful effect…this excellence the groups of Raphael share with the antique.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful work must register as a harmonious, balanced form even from afar; first-glance architectural/ornamental effect and balance of forms are essential qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine enthusiasm vs performative praise
rubrics_metrics.description: “Genuine enthusiasm, however crude…always elevates… but…talking and writing for effect stultifies and debases.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish authentic public appreciation from fashionable, drawing-room, or newspaper-driven rapture; genuine admiration aids artistic culture, while performative praise misleads and debases standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and impartial committee for public commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The dignified way…would be to have a committee chosen of impartial judges, men who would look only to the merits of the work and the interests of the country, unbiassed by any personal interest in favor of some one artist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public monumental commissions should be decided by impartial juries focused solely on artistic merit; avoid nepotism, petty jealousies, and private influence. Solicit designs from multiple artists and choose the best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple competent artists to receive public commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I admire various excellences in the works of each, and should be glad if each received an order for an equestrian statue…There is money enough in the country, and the more good things there are for the people to see freely… the better.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where resources permit, commissioning several accomplished artists benefits the public and stimulates artistic growth—do not concentrate patronage to the detriment of broader cultural enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of allegory and supporting figures in monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense of Crawford’s group: the winged figure “not only gives a poetic sense to the group, but a natural support and occasion for action to the horse and rider.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical or supporting figures should serve a natural compositional and narrative function, giving poetic sense and structural balance rather than imposing insipid or overwrought symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of conception (artistic thought) and technical execution
rubrics_metrics.description: On Powers: “His conception of what is individual in character is clear and just, his power of execution almost unrivalled; but…his studies on the human body are comparatively limited… his conception of subject is not striking: I do not consider him rich in artistic thought.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great sculpture requires both compelling artistic conception (richness of subject and thought) and mastery of execution (anatomy, freedom, technical command); excellence in one cannot fully substitute for deficiency in the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for adequate payment covering design time, materials, and labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Patrons often ignore “that the painter, the sculptor, must be paid for the time he spends in designing and moulding, no less than in painting and carving; that he must have his bread…his marbles and colors…the sculptor his workmen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons should pay fairly for all aspects of artistic production (design, modeling, materials, studio, assistants). Underpaying or bargaining down prices denies artists fair recompense for their thought and labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid changing patron’s mind after work is modelled
rubrics_metrics.description: “The American Mæcenas sometimes, after ordering a work, has been known to change his mind when the statue is already modelled.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons should understand the commitment they make: changing requirements after substantial work has been done is unjust to the artist and wastes resources—contracts and clear expectations are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations about artists’ living costs in Europe
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorandum: “The rent of a suitable studio…$200 a year. The best journeyman carver…$60 a month. Models are paid $1 a day.…for a statue of life-size the demand is from $1,000 to $5,000…$1,000 per annum should be placed at the disposal of every young artist leaving our country for Europe.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons and prospective students should recognize the true expenses of artistic study and production abroad; the notion that one can live on $300–$400 a year is erroneous—adequate funding is necessary for serious study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patron education and sympathy as obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: To supply means of judging to the American merchant who wants pictures and statues, the author provides cost data and criticizes ignorance and bargain-hunting which harm artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons should educate themselves about artistic processes and costs, approach commissions with sympathy and fair-mindedness rather than seeking bargains at artists’ expense, and value the artist’s intellectual contribution, not only material product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject choice for national monuments should reflect national virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: “Everything concurs to make an equestrian statue of Washington desirable…To present the man on horseback…may well be deemed a high achievement of modern, as it was of ancient art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects for public monuments that embody national character and dignity; the subject should also be suitable to the medium (e.g., equestrian statue suits a commander like Washington).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic vocation over material gain
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is particularly gratifying to see men that might amass far more money…and aim only at excellence in the expression of thought.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True artistic excellence often requires prioritizing expression and integrity over financial reward; patronage should support this vocation rather than pressure artists toward commercial compromises.
